script.dialogo:
FILIPPO: today we're looking at every Italian student's annual nightmare: the end of summer. The 2026/2027 school year is officially kicking off across the country, putting an end to those long fourteen weeks of summer breaks, but as with most things in Italy, there isn't a single national opening day. (coperture studenti)

ARDE: (lavagna italia) Non-uniformity! That is the secret, Filippo! Italian pupils enjoy an average of 14 continuous weeks of summer vacation—that's roughly 2,352 hours of gelato, sea salt, and absolute bliss! But starting September 7th in Bolzano, up until September 17th in Puglia, 20 distinct regional calendars will break this summer entropy over a ten-day staggered window!

FILIPPO: while kids in South Tyrol are already sitting at their desks, students in Bari still have over a week of beach time left. But once everyone is finally back in the classroom, the real psychological challenge begins: the autumn 2026 calendar is mathematically brutal, with almost every major holiday landing directly on a weekend and wiping out potential long breaks.

ARDE: A statistical nightmare! San Francesco on October 4th? Sunday! All Saints' Day on November 1st? Sunday! Total weekend overlap! The probability of an autumn ponte—or bridge holiday—is currently sitting at a devastating zero percent until December 8th!

FILIPPO: A long wait until the Immaculate Conception in December, which thankfully lands on a Tuesday to give everyone a proper four-day weekend. Meanwhile, high school seniors across Italy are already looking past winter and Easter toward the ultimate final hurdle: the national written exam starting precisely on Wednesday, June 16th, 2027.

ARDE: Ah, La Maturità! The finish line of Italian adolescence! The countdown is ticking: exactly 200 mandatory teaching days stand between thousands of eighteen-year-olds and their final Italian essay!

FILIPPO: We wish the very best of luck to all students, teachers, and parents navigating the staggered chaos and surviving the long autumn ahead

FILIPPO: Roma gets dressed up for the arts — the Romaeuropa Festival is back, running from September 8th all the way to November 15th, spreading across 20 venues in the Eternal City. Contemporary creation, international stages, and that very Roman mix of chaos and genius.

ARDE: Exactly, Filippo — 20 spaces, 68 days of programming, and this is the 41st edition, which they're calling RE41F. That's four decades of bringing the world's avant-garde to a city where the Colosseum is basically the warm-up act.

FILIPPO: Forty-one years of this festival means it started in 1985 — when shoulder pads were a personality and contemporary dance was considered dangerous. Rome has changed. The shoulder pads, thankfully, less so.

ARDE: And if you do the math, 20 venues across 68 days means Rome is essentially one giant theatre for over two months. My solution? Move in. Sublet your apartment and live in a different venue each week — culturally optimal, financially terrifying.

FILIPPO: Trending number two!

ARDE: This, Filippo, is the flag of Slovakia! White, blue and red — classic Pan-Slavic colours, with a very special coat of arms right in the middle.

FILIPPO: A double cross on three hills — it looks almost like a medieval emblem. Very proud, very dignified!

ARDE: Today Slovakia celebrates the Day of Our Lady of Sorrows — their national patron — and it is also the country's official national holiday. A beautiful blend of spirituality and national pride!

FILIPPO: I love that a country chooses a feast of compassion and reflection as its national day. There's something very poetic about that.

ARDE: Very poetic indeed! And Slovakia itself is full of surprises. Did you know it holds a rather extraordinary European record? Its capital Bratislava is the only capital city in the world that borders TWO other sovereign countries — Austria and Hungary — at the same time!

FILIPPO: No! A capital city with two international borders? That is genuinely remarkable. Professor, show us on the map!

ARDE: Here it is — smack in the southwest corner of the country! Bratislava hugs the Danube river, with Austria literally a few kilometres to the west and Hungary just across the river to the south. Vienna is closer to Bratislava than many Slovak cities are. It's one of the most fascinating geographical situations in all of Europe!

FILIPPO: A capital at the edge of the world — or rather, at the crossroads of three worlds! Alright everyone, stay with us — it's time for the domandone!

bandierina.dialogo:
ARDE: This, Filippo, is the flag of Tonga – a vivid red with a white rectangle in the corner and a bright red cross. It has been flying proudly since 1875!

FILIPPO: 1875 – so the flag is older than many European republics! And today Tonga is celebrating the Birthday of the Crown Prince – a national holiday full of festivities.

ARDE: Exactly! Now, Tonga is not just one island – it is an entire archipelago, and a rather fascinating one geographically. It spans both sides of the International Date Line, making it one of the first places on Earth to greet each new day.

FILIPPO: So Tongans are literally the first people to say good morning to the world every single day – I love that! The 'Kingdom of the Sunrise', in a way.

ARDE: Beautifully put! And here is my geographical puzzle for you, Filippo: Tonga is made up of island groups – the Tongatapu group in the south, the Ha'apai group in the middle, and the Vava'u group in the north. But can you guess roughly how many islands in total make up the kingdom?

FILIPPO: Oh, that is a very good question – I want to say… a lot? Let our audience decide! But first, Professor, show us where this kingdom of early mornings actually sits on the map!

ARDE: Right here in the South Pacific – east of Fiji, north of New Zealand, and just west of the International Date Line. A necklace of islands stretching about 800 kilometres from north to south, entirely within Polynesia.

FILIPPO: Eight hundred kilometres of paradise – and now, dear friends at home, it is time for the domandone!

ARDE: This, Filippo, is the flag of Chile — red, white, blue, and that iconic lone star at its heart. They call it La Estrella Solitaria — the Lone Star.

FILIPPO: The Lone Star! And today, the 18th of September, all of Chile is celebrating — dancing cueca, eating empanadas, and toasting with a good pisco sour!

ARDE: Now, Filippo, here is something that genuinely astonishes me about Chile. Geographically, it may be the most extreme country on the planet. It spans no fewer than 38 degrees of latitude.

FILIPPO: Thirty-eight degrees of latitude! That means in one single country you can go from one of the driest places on Earth to some of the coldest, wettest landscapes imaginable?

ARDE: Absolutely! The Atacama Desert in the north receives virtually no rainfall — some weather stations there have never recorded any. And in the far south, Chilean Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego are permanently battered by Antarctic winds and glaciers. One country, every climate.

FILIPPO: Desert, vineyards, volcanoes, glaciers — and all of it squeezed into that incredible narrow strip! Now, Professor, show us where this extraordinary ribbon of land actually is on the map!

ARDE: Right here — clinging to the western edge of South America, with the mighty Andes running along its entire eastern border and the vast Pacific Ocean to the west. From top to bottom, Chile stretches over 4,300 kilometres — making it roughly the distance from London to Baghdad, all in one country!

FILIPPO: London to Baghdad — in one country! That is extraordinary. And now, it is absolutely time for our domandone for the audience!

Exactly! And that date, the 18th of September 1810, marks something very precise in history — not yet full independence, but the creation of the very first self-governing body: the Primera Junta Nacional de Gobierno.
So it's the birthday of Chilean self-government, not just independence! That's a subtle but fascinating distinction, Professor.
Precisely! And the Junta, mind you, initially claimed to be governing in the name of the Spanish King Ferdinand VII — who was Napoleon's prisoner at the time. History loves its little ironies.
Governing for a king who was in chains — remarkable! Now, Professor, show us where Chile actually sits on the map!

Here it is — the southwestern coast of South America, a long, extraordinary ribbon of land squeezed between the Andes to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the west. From the driest desert on Earth in the north, the Atacama, all the way down to wild Patagonia and the tip of the continent in the south.
Desert to glaciers, all in one country — incredible! And speaking of incredible, it's time for our domandone for the audience!

sections.title: SONIA CANDY CAFFE'

script.dialogo:
FILIPPO: Sonia!

SONIA: Hi Filippo! Hi Professor

FILIPPO: Welcome back! We're so happy to have you here again this year.

SONIA: I'm so happy to be back! I missed you guys!

ARDE: We missed you too! So, Sonia, today we're talking about something VERY important in Italy…

ARDE: Coffee!

SONIA: Of course!

FILIPPO: And more specifically, the Italian bar. Because this can be a little confusing for foreigners, right?

SONIA: Absolutely! Because if you tell an English speaker, "I'm going to the bar," they'll probably imagine a place where you go at night. Music, cocktails, maybe a few drinks…

FILIPPO: Maybe some dancing?

SONIA: Maybe! But an Italian bar is completely different. You can go there at seven in the morning!

ARDE: Hopefully not for a cocktail.

SONIA: I mean… I'm not judging! But usually you go there for coffee, breakfast, a cornetto… You might also have an aperitivo later in the day, but it's not what an English speaker normally imagines when they hear the word bar.

FILIPPO: So what would you call an Italian bar in English?

SONIA: There isn't really a perfect translation. Depending on the place, you might say café or coffee shop, but the Italian bar is really its own thing.

FILIPPO: And then there's Italian coffee culture.

SONIA: Yes! Because if you walk into an Italian bar and say, "Un caffè," what do you get?

ARDE: An espresso!

SONIA: Exactly. In Italy, caffè basically means espresso by default. A tiny cup, very strong coffee… and sometimes the whole experience lasts about thirty seconds.

FILIPPO: Very different from American coffee culture.

SONIA: VERY different. In the US, you might walk around for an hour with a huge coffee in your hand. And the order can be… complicated.

ARDE: Complicated how?

SONIA: "Can I get a large iced vanilla latte with oat milk, an extra shot, sugar-free syrup, light ice—"

ARDE: Stop! I'm already tired.

SONIA: Exactly! In a traditional Italian bar, things tend to be much simpler.

FILIPPO: Okay, Sonia. Teach us! What are some classic Italian coffee drinks?

SONIA: Okay! First, espresso — what Italians normally call caffè. Then caffè macchiato: espresso with just a little bit of milk or milk foam.

ARDE: And cappuccino?

SONIA: Espresso with steamed milk and foam. And then there's caffellatte, which has much more milk and is usually associated with breakfast.

ARDE: So… cappuccino after dinner?

SONIA: You CAN. The police will not arrest you.

ARDE: But the Italians might judge you.

SONIA: Oh, they WILL judge you.

FILIPPO: So, lesson of the day?

SONIA: If an Italian says, "Let's meet at the bar for a coffee," don't show up at a nightclub expecting a caramel frappuccino!

FILIPPO: Got it!

sections.title: VEG OF THE WEEK: FIG

script.dialogo:
FILIPPO: Professor, this week's veg is the fig — il fico — and I have to say, Italy and figs go back a very, very long way. In fact, if you look closely at ancient Rome, the whole empire was basically running on them! Legend has it that Romulus and Remus were nursed by the she-wolf right under a Ficus Ruminalis. Pliny the Elder was practically obsessed, documenting over 29 different varieties, and Cato used a fresh fig from Carthage in the Senate just to prove how close and dangerous the enemy was! So, in a way, figs didn't just feed the country — they literally shaped Roman history.

ARDE: (LAVAGNA ITALIA)Filippo, you have no idea. The fig tree, Ficus carica, is one of the first plants ever cultivated by humans — some archaeobotanists date domesticated fig remains to around 11,400 years ago, which is older than wheat or barley. Italy is currently among the top European producers, with Calabria and Puglia leading the harvest.

FILIPPO: So basically, before Italians invented pasta, they had already figured out the fig. Somehow that feels right! And it's not just history, it’s alive and kicking right now. Look at Cilento, where the *Fico Bianco del Cilento DOP* is practically an institution. In Carmignano, Tuscany, they have a dedicated *Fico Secco* Slow Food Presidium. And in southern news, chefs are even experimenting with zero-waste fig oil pressed from the seeds, plus wild fig leaf oil to make gelato with a fresh, coconut-and-grass note!

ARDE: Precisely. And here is a surreal thought: fresh figs are roughly 80% water, yet they are one of the highest plant sources of calcium — more calcium per 100 grams than most vegetables. My proposal, Filippo, is that you replace your morning coffee with ten raw figs and report back to the studio in six weeks.

FILIPPO: Ten figs at 7 a.m. — I'll take that under advisement, Professor. But if we’re talking real menus, I’d much rather build a proper feast around them!

**Antipasto:** Warm crostini with creamy Gorgonzola dolce, fresh Black Mission figs, a drizzle of chestnut honey, and a crack of black pepper. Or the classic *Fichi e Prosciutto di Parma*, but grilled for 30 seconds so the caramel sugars bleed into the ham.
* **Primo:** Hand-rolled tagliolini with guanciale, fresh figs cooked down into a glossy, savory glaze, finished with aged Pecorino Romano.
* **Secondo:** Pork tenderloin roasted with fresh figs, rosemary, and a heavy splash of Balsamic Vinegar of Modena DOP.
* **Dolce:** A classic *Torta di Fichi e Noci* — a rustica tart filled with fresh figs, chopped walnuts, and a hint of lemon zest, served with a scoop of fig-leaf infuised gelato.

FILIPPO: Grappolo d'Oro — sounds like something you'd win at a wine festival in Tuscany, and honestly, that's not far off. But today the article that was supposed to tell us the story... arrived as pure JavaScript code. The content got lost somewhere between a PHP session and a Google Tag Manager container.

ARDE: Filippo, technically what we received contains exactly 2 GTM container IDs, 1 session sync handler, and 0 — zero — actual words of journalism. That is a data-to-content ratio of infinity to one, which is statistically unprecedented in the history of this show.

FILIPPO: So the Golden Grape remains a mystery. Is it a wine award? A variety? A metaphor for Italian excellence? We may never know, because the internet decided to send us its plumbing instead of its poetry.

ARDE: My professional recommendation: we award the Grappolo d'Oro to whoever wrote that sync.php script — they clearly worked harder than the journalist. And Filippo should celebrate with a glass of whatever this grape belongs to, assuming it exists.

FILIPPO: On that note of digital surrealism — Trending n° 2!

FILIPPO: Philosophy meets the piazza — and not just in lecture halls. The Festivalfilosofia spreads across three cities: Modena, Carpi, and Sassuolo. Thousands of Italians literally sit on the street to think. Imagine that.

ARDE: And the 2026 edition already has a full PDF program, a creative program, a kids program, and something called 'Cucina Filosofica' — which I calculate is the only festival where Kant and tortellini share equal billing.

FILIPPO: Cucina Filosofica — I love that. You eat, you think, you question whether the tortellino was ever truly al dente, or merely performing al dente-ness.

ARDE: Exactly. Heidegger would say the tortellino reveals its being only in the boiling. I would say the festival, spanning 3 cities simultaneously, is statistically the widest outdoor philosophy event in Italy — though I admit that is a very specific ranking.

FILIPPO: A festival where the whole town becomes a classroom. That's genuinely beautiful — and very Italian. Trending number two!

script.dialogo:
FILIPPO: Trending number three! Italian students are now officially above the OECD average in reading, mathematics, and science — according to the PISA 2025 results. Minister Valditara says Italy is becoming an international reference point. Not bad for a country that invented the Renaissance, right?

ARDE: Filippo, three subjects above the OECD average simultaneously — that is statistically significant. In mathematics, Italy scored 487, up from 471 in 2022. In reading, 489. The OECD average hovers around 481. These are real gaps, not rounding errors.

FILIPPO: And yet every Italian parent still thinks their child's school is a disaster. It's a national sport — complaining about the system while the system quietly wins.

ARDE: A classic Italian paradox. The data improves; the pessimism remains constant. Perhaps pessimism is what drives the improvement. My constant work may have helped somehow.

script.intervista:
FILIPPO: Hi Luca, welcome back! We’re heading into autumn. Let’s watch a clip we’ve put together. What’s happening in Stelvio National Park?

LUCA: Hi Paparazzi, hi Filippo, hi Marco!
Right now, a lot is happening in Stelvio National Park!
It’s a very interesting transition period: nature is changing its rhythm, and every animal is facing the arrival of the cold season with different strategies.

FILIPPO: What do you mean?

LUCA: Some animals are preparing for a season of intense activity, namely the breeding season.
Others, on the other hand, are getting ready for a much quieter season.
Take the marmot, for example: it is heading toward hibernation.
 At this time of year, it is still feeding and trying to accumulate as much fat reserve as possible.
 Then, when the cold weather arrives, it retreats into its burrow and greatly slows down all its vital functions.
 Its body temperature drops, its heart rate and breathing slow down, and its metabolism is drastically reduced.
 In this way, it can consume the reserves accumulated during the summer very slowly and survive the months when food virtually disappears.
And to do this, it needs a very special shelter.
Marmots have a complex burrow system that they use throughout the year, but in different ways depending on the season.
 Summer burrows are generally shallower and may have several exits, which are also useful for quickly escaping predators.
 The winter burrow, on the other hand, is much deeper and more protected: it may have a single access tunnel several meters long.
 At the end of the tunnel there is a real chamber, carefully lined with dry grass.
 Before winter, the entrance is sealed off, creating a protected environment where the marmot can spend several months.
Hibernation generally lasts from autumn until March or April, depending on environmental conditions.

FILIPPO: I like marmots! But explain to me why they whistle and what this behavior represents.

LUCA: Actually, what we call a “whistle” is not really a whistle: it’s an alarm call.
 The marmot produces a very high-pitched and easily recognizable sound.
 Its main purpose is to warn other marmots of a potential danger.
 When a marmot spots a predator, or something it interprets as a threat, it emits this call and the others can quickly take refuge in their burrows.
 It is therefore a very important social behavior: one marmot that sees danger can effectively alert the entire group.
There is also something interesting: these calls can vary depending on the type of threat and the situation. So it’s not simply a generic alarm, but part of a rather sophisticated
communication system.

FILIPPO: Luca, what scientific projects are you currently working on?

LUCA: At the moment, we are observing and monitoring various aspects of the biology and behavior of the animals living in the Park.
 One of the things that particularly interests us is understanding how animals are responding to environmental changes.
 Climate change does not simply mean higher temperatures: it means changes in the rhythm of the seasons, food availability, snow cover duration, and therefore the conditions in which animals live.
 For this reason, we monitor behaviors, animal conditions, and important stages of their biological cycles over time.
 The goal is to understand not only what is changing, but also how different species can—or cannot—adapt to these changes.

FILIPPO: So climate change also affects these behaviors?

LUCA: Unfortunately, yes, and perhaps this is one of the most interesting aspects to observe.
 Animals have developed their biological cycles by following the rhythm of the seasons throughout evolution.
 If that rhythm changes, fundamental behaviors may also change: when to hibernate, when to emerge from hibernation, when to reproduce, or when food is most available.
 The problem arises especially when two events that used to be perfectly synchronized are no longer aligned.
 For example, an animal may breed earlier because spring arrives sooner, but if the availability of its main food source does not advance in the same way, it may face
difficulties.
That is precisely why scientific monitoring is so important: it allows us to detect these changes and understand which species are most vulnerable.
FILIPPO: Come on, give me at least one piece of good news! Do deer still fall in love?
ARDE: Now that’s important: one certainty!

LUCA: Yes, let’s just say that at this time of year, deer definitely have something else on their minds!
With the beginning of the breeding season comes the rutting season, one of the great natural spectacles of autumn in the Park.
 Males approach groups of females and try to attract their attention.
 They do so mainly through roaring, or rutting calls, which are powerful and distinctive vocalizations.
 But it is not only a way to attract females: the roar also serves to communicate a male’s presence and status to other males.
 It is therefore also a form of competition: males often try to avoid physical confrontation by using their size, posture, and especially their vocalizations to establish who is stronger.
It is a period when deer behavior changes completely, and the Park’s landscape fills with these sounds.

FILIPPO: And then what happens? When are the fawns born?

LUCA: After the breeding season, you have to wait several months.
 Births generally occur between late May and June.
 Normally, only one fawn is born.
 During the first months, the fawn has its characteristic brown coat with white spots.
 These spots contribute to camouflage and make the youngster very difficult to spot when it remains motionless among the grass and vegetation.
And this is where there is an important message to remember when we are in the mountains.
The mother, especially during the first weeks, may leave the fawn hidden alone for several hours and return periodically to nurse it.
So if, during a hike, we come across a young animal that appears to be alone, this does not mean it has been abandoned.
The best thing we can do is: 
 not approach it;
 not touch it;
 not pick it up;
 not take it away;
 calmly move on and let the mother take care of it.

Our intervention, even with the best intentions, can interfere with the mother’s normal behavior and put the youngster at risk.
So the rule is very simple: if we find a young wild animal, the best thing we can do is leave it where it is.

FILIPPO: So, to sum up: the marmot is going to sleep, while the deer is in the middle of the mating season. What should we do?

LUCA: Above all, we should observe without disturbing.
 The mountains are the animals’ home, and we are guests.
 We can listen to the deer’s rutting calls, watch marmots while they are active, and encounter many other species.
 But we must leave animals their space and their time.
And that is precisely one of the reasons why Parks exist: to allow us to get to know nature while protecting it at the same time.

Luca  Corlatti, Scientific coordinator for Stelvio Park in Lombardy Region, where he lworks for Office of Scientific Research and Our activities focusing on biodiversity and climate change monitoring, relationships between biodiversity abd human-environment and applied applied research on keystone Alpine species, which includes Cervus Elaphus, the Red Deer, Cervo Nobile in italian. Deer had (almost) completely disappeared from Italy after World War II.
 Now the species is in a good state of conservation. The deer is the largest wild ruminant herbivore in Italy. In many areas, especially in parks and protected areas, numbers and densities are very high. This has a significant impact on vegetation, so much so that the deer is referred to as the engineer of ecosystems. Now, with the spontaneous return of the wolf to the Alps, we are entering a new phase of ecosystem balance. The arrival of the predator may change the numbers and behavior of prey, and this, in turn, may have an effect on vegetation. The study of trophic cascades in parks and its usefulness.

FIlippo: The Chapel of the Princes, the museum’s monumental Baroque heart, was conceived based on an idea by Cosimo I de’ Medici as a place dedicated to the glorification of the grand ducal branch of the dynasty. The six side walls are clad in polychrome marble and semi-precious stones and house the large commemorative sarcophagi of the sovereigns, above which are niches intended for their monumental gilded bronze effigies. However, the project remained unfinished, and only the statues of Ferdinand I—who founded the chapel in 1603—and his son Cosimo II were actually completed.

The  museum is part of the Galleria dell’Accademia di Firenze and  Musei del Bargello group of the Ministry of Culture. script.dialogo:
FILIPPO: Oliver Stone turns 80 in Rome — not bad for a man who spent decades making Hollywood nervous. The Casa del Cinema rolled out the red carpet for the director of Platoon, JFK, and Wall Street. Rome choosing him, or him choosing Rome?

ARDE: Statistically speaking, Filippo, Oliver Stone has directed 24 feature films over a career spanning 50 years. That is one film every 2.08 years — a pace that puts him well above the industry average for directors of his generation.

FILIPPO: And there is something very Italian about celebrating an American rebel at a villa in Rome. The Casa del Cinema sits inside Villa Borghese — arguably the most cinematic park in the world.

ARDE: Villa Borghese covers 80 hectares — one for each year of Stone's life, which I find either poetic or a coincidence, and I refuse to decide which. I will say that at 80, Stone has outlived three of his own controversial film controversies.

FILIPPO: Ha! Rome has a way of making everything feel less controversial and more eternal. Happy birthday, Oliver — benvenuto all'80. Trending number two!

The first edition of Francesissimo — a mirror and complementary project to Italissimo, which for ten years has brought Italian literature and culture to Paris — will take place in Turin from 30 January to 1 February 2026, bringing the French literature and culture festival to the city: meetings with French and francophone authors and author-esses, readings and film screenings, designed to foster dialogue between the cultural world across the Alps and the Italian public.
Francesissimo, conceived by the Fondazione Circolo dei Lettori and the Consulate General of France in Milan, and curated by Fabio Gambaro, will be held at the Circolo dei Lettori e delle Lettrici, Cinema Massimo, Alliance Française Torino, and the Biblioteca Civica Centrale.
The festival opens with Daniel Pennac. It closes with Boualem Sansal: his first public appearance following the pardon he received on 12 November last year from his country, Algeria, where he had been imprisoned since November 2024 for “undermining national unity”.

It is the successor to Take Our Daughters To Work Day, which was expanded to include boys in 2003. In the U.S., it occurs on the fourth Thursday in April every year.

International No Diet Day (INDD) is an annual celebration of body acceptance, including fat acceptance and body shape diversity. This day is also dedicated to promoting a healthy life style with a focus on health at any size and in raising awareness of the potential dangers of dieting and the unlikelihood of success; the Institute of Medicine summarises: "those who complete weight loss programs lose approximately 10 percent of their body weight only to regain two-thirds within a year and almost all of it within five years." The first International No Diet Day was celebrated in the UK in 1992. Feminist groups in other countries around the globe have started to celebrate International No Diet Day, especially in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Israel, Denmark, Sweden and Brazil.

International No Diet Day (INDD) is an annual celebration of body acceptance, including fat acceptance and body shape diversity. The first International No Diet Day was celebrated in the UK in 1992. Feminist groups in other countries around the globe have started to celebrate International No Diet Day, especially in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Israel, Denmark, Sweden and Brazil.

Basato sull'evento 274 anni fa (1752).

Global Wind Day or World Wind Day is a worldwide event that is held on June 15 around the world. It is organised by WindEurope and GWEC .
 It is a day when wind energy is celebrated, information is exchanged and adults and children find out about wind energy, its power and the possibilities it holds to change the world. 
In association with EWEA and GWEC, national wind energy associations and companies involved in wind energy production organise events in many countries around the world. In 2011, there were events organised in 30 countries, on 4 continents. Events included visits to onshore and offshore wind farms, information campaigns, demonstration turbines being set up in cities, wind workshops and a wind parade. Many events happened on Global Wind Day itself, but there were also events on the days and weeks before and afterwards. In 2012 there were 250 events around the globe and a very popular photo competition.

La Festa del Torrone chiude a Camerino il periodo natalizio nel giorno dell’Epifania. Tra storia ducale, tradizione camerte e grande taglio del maxi torrone, il dolce simbolo della città diventa rito collettivo.
calEvents.title: XXV Festa del Torrone

calEvents.note: La Festa della Cicerchia accende Serra de’ Conti con fuochi, taverne, profumi e voci. Il legume antico del borgo diventa protagonista di piatti semplici e sorprendenti, tra vicoli, cantine e spazi storici.

Appassimenti Aperti apre a Serrapetrona i luoghi dove la Vernaccia Nera riposa sospesa. Cantine, degustazioni e racconti dei produttori svelano le due anime del territorio: Vernaccia DOCG e Serrapetrona DOC.
calEvents.title: Appassimenti Aperti

guests.bio: Fabio Testi is the star who turned his good looks from a supposed “flaw” into a ticket to cinematic legend. Born in Peschiera del Garda, he started out as a stuntman — falling off horses, crashing motorbikes, and even hanging in midair for two weeks on the set of Barbarella. It was Vittorio De Sica who catapulted him to fame with the Oscar-winning The Garden of the Finzi-Continis in 1970. From there came a career packed with auteur films and popular hits (Addio fratello crudele, L’important c’est d’aimer with Romy Schneider, Camorra by Pasquale Squitieri), over a hundred screen and stage credits, and a love life straight out of the tabloids — Ursula Andress, Anita Ekberg, Charlotte Rampling, Edwige Fenech… Today, well into his eighties, Testi still keeps us guessing: he grows truffles by Lake Garda, tours with a poetry-and-music show, and pops up in international cinema — most recently in Reflet dans un diamant mort, which premiered at the Berlinale. Always elegant, always magnetic, he’s living proof that yes, there really are a few beautiful men who are also smart. His research interests are molecular ecology, population genetics and phylogeny of marine organisms. He study mainly fish and sharks, from coastal to the deep-sea, but he's been a guest of Paparazzi helping our understanding of marine alien species in our seas like the lionfish and the silver-cheeked toadfish. ANDREA LEVY: Andrea Levy was born in Ancona on July 7, 1971. He specialized in international marketing and communication at the University of Nevada. His passion for cars has been with him since childhood. He grew up in Moncalieri, near Turin, where he saw prototypes and cars from legendary coachbuilders and manufacturers—Pininfarina, Giugiaro, Italdesign, and Fiat—come to life and hit the roads. Today, he is a successful entrepreneur in communication and events, a devoted collector of sports cars and supercars, and a true motorsport enthusiast. He races with Ferrari Club Italia and competes in Time Attack with Ferrari, Radical, and Dallara. Always on the move, he follows racing competitions, auto shows, and dynamic events such as Goodwood and Pebble Beach—experiences that sparked the idea behind the Salone dell'Auto format, which has now also evolved into the Milano Monza Motor Show.

guests.bio: Luca Bruschi is the director of AEVF, European Association of the Via Francigena Ways. As Director, Bruschi is at the forefront of the nomination of the Via Francigena as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July, the preliminary dossier was officially submitted in Paris, focusing on the Italian section of the route from the Great St. Bernard Pass to Rome. The next stage of the candidacy will begin at the end of September 2025: this phase involves compiling the final dossier, identifying the cultural assets to be included on the UNESCO list, producing detailed cartography, and organizing participatory meetings with local communities along the route.The Via Francigena is certified Cultural Route of the Council of Europe. More than 3000 kilometers, from Canterbury to Rome and Santa Maria di Leuca, to walk step by step on mountain paths, mule tracks, rural and secondary roads, cypress-lined dirt roads or among majestic pines. Bruschi has personally completed the Via Francigena, the Camino de Santiago, and many other pilgrimage routes and cultural itineraries across Europe.

Deer had (almost) completely disappeared from Italy after World War II.
 Now the species is in a good state of conservation. The deer is the largest wild ruminant herbivore in Italy. In many areas, especially in parks and protected areas, numbers and densities are very high. This has a significant impact on vegetation, so much so that the deer is referred to as the engineer of ecosystems. Now, with the spontaneous return of the wolf to the Alps, we are entering a new phase of ecosystem balance. The arrival of the predator may change the numbers and behavior of prey, and this, in turn, may have an effect on vegetation. The study of trophic cascades in parks and its usefulness.

guests.bio: My name is Valerio Minato, born in Biella in 1981, and I discovered photography in 2012, almost by chance, as a passion that began during the final stages of my studies in Forestry and Environmental Sciences at the University of Turin. What started as a hobby soon grew into a true vocation: inspired by my love for Turin, the city that adopted me, I began capturing its panoramas and iconic views with increasing dedication and success. A self-taught photographer, I have developed a personal style that combines innovative shooting angles and daring perspectives, offering fresh and original interpretations of familiar landscapes. My academic background, along with a strong passion for geography and cartography, often guides me in the search for unique vantage points and striking visual alignments—for example, photographing Monviso and the Milan skyline from the Bergamo province. Over the years, my projects and images have gained recognition and have been featured in major online outlets and national newspapers, including *La Stampa, Repubblica,* and *Tuttosport*.

Luca Morino, born in Turin in 1962, is an Italian singer, composer, writer, and cultural promoter. He is the founder and lead singer of Mau Mau, a band that blends folk, African rhythms, and sonic contaminations. He has also released solo projects such as Mistic Turistic, Vox Creola, and, in 2024, DeWest. DeWest is a journey into the Far West — an oneiric, deconstructed territory ideally located in the Lower Piedmont region,  which corresponds, in a disorienting geography, to the Alta Langa area. The music of DeWest could be described, if such a genre existed, as voodoo folk: cinematic, expansive, yet also ritualistic, almost sacred, though within a secular vision. Beyond music, he writes, curates columns, and takes part in cultural initiatives in Piedmont and beyond.

guests.bio: Matteo Strukul is an Italian novelist, journalist, and screenwriter. He holds a degree in Law, a PhD in European Law, and is a former member of the Historical Novel Society. His works are being published in forty countries and have been optioned for film adaptations. In 2017, he won the prestigious Premio Bancarella for I Medici: Una dinastia al potere (The Medici: Ascendancy of a Family).  Beyond novels, Strukul has written graphic novels (including a trilogy on Vlad the Impaler) and works as a screenwriter. Strukul is artistic director of Chronicae, International Festival of Historical Novel (16 - 19 Aprile 2026, Piove di Sacco -PD). He divides his time between Padua, Milan, and Berlin — and occasionally, Transylvania.

guests.sottopancia: Assoc. Prof. of Contemporary History UNISG, writer
guests.bio:
"Porta Palazzo - Storia orale e sensoriale del mercato più grande d’Europa" (Donzelli Ed.) Since 1835, Turin’s Porta Palazzo market has been a hub for observing the city’s social, cultural, and urban changes. A daily resource for working-class communities, it fosters transcultural encounters where diverse food practices and knowledge evolve. A destination for migrants from Piedmont, southern Italy, Africa, Asia, and Latin America, it embodies historical and diasporic layers, blending global and local dynamics. Through over 200 interviews with vendors, customers, and Turin’s diasporic communities, Gabriele Proglio crafts a narrative using food as a memory tool, capturing sensory recollections and emotions. In this liminal space, individual and collective stories intertwine, reflecting a city where past, present, and future meet at the market stalls.
Gabriele Proglio is an assoc. prof. of Contemporary History at the University of Gastronomic Sciences in Pollenzo. He has worked at the University of California, Berkeley, the European University Institute, Université El Manar in Tunis, and the universities of Coimbra, Ankara, and Grenoble. Among his recent publications in the field of oral history are The Horn of Africa Diasporas in Italy: An Oral History (Palgrave, 2020) and I fatti di Genova (Donzelli, 2021).

guests.bio: Iuri Moscardi is a PhD candidate in Comparative Literature (Italian Specialization) at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York. He studied Cesare Pavese during his years at Università degli Studi di Milano: his Bachelor degree thesis focused on the end of the American myth in The Moon and the Bonfires and his Master degree thesis, awarded with the Premio Pavese 2012, analyzed the typescript of the first Italian translation of Spoon River Anthology, proving the role of Pavese as editor of Fernanda Pivano’s translation. After having obtained his Master degree, he moved to the United States and in 2016 he received a Master of Arts in Italian from Indiana University, Bloomington. Since 2012, he has been involved in the digital social reading experiments of TwLetteratura and Betwyll, at the center of his dissertation research. He edited the collection of essays Cesare Pavese Mythographer, Translator, Modernist: A Collection of Studies 70 Years after His Death (2023) and the new, complete English translation of Pavese’s Mestiere di vivere (2025). He has also published articles and essays, in journals and volumes, in Italian and English, focused on Pavese and contemporary Italian literature. For Fondazione Cesare Pavese he is created "Dialoghi con Pavese", a bilingual column with interviews to Pavese's scholars around the world and the series of video interviews "Io vengo di là – Qualcosa di molto serio e prezioso" and "Un Pavese ci vuole". He conducted a research on the books donated by the Molina family to Fondazione Cesare Pavese, published on the academic journal Italica and presented during a symposium at New York University in 2023. As a freelance journalist, he writes about cultural and literary topics on La Lettura, Giornale di Brescia, Il Foglio, and il manifesto.

guests.bio: "Can I take a photo of your dog?" is the question Navid Tarazi uses to approach every human–animal pair. From that simple phrase was born @doggodaiily, the photographic project that has become a hugely popular page on Instagram and TikTok, where Navid tells the stories of the dogs he meets every day. From there also comes the book “Can I take a photo of your dog?”, published by Mondadori Electa, a volume that collects the portraits and stories of the many dogs and owners encountered by chance on the street. Navid Tarazi is an Iranian guy who moved to Italy in 2022. He studies Environmental Engineering at the Politecnico di Torino and has a passion for photography. In his home country, dogs are not considered pets, so while walking the streets of Italy, Navid is struck by the affectionate relationships he sees between four-legged friends and humans, and he wants to better understand the canine world.

guests.bio: My name is Valerio Minato, born in Biella in 1981, and I discovered photography in 2012, almost by chance, as a passion that began during the final stages of my studies in Forestry and Environmental Sciences at the University of Turin. What started as a hobby soon grew into a true vocation: inspired by my love for Turin, the city that adopted me, I began capturing its panoramas and iconic views with increasing dedication and success. A self-taught photographer, I have developed a personal style that combines innovative shooting angles and daring perspectives, offering fresh and original interpretations of familiar landscapes. My academic background, along with a strong passion for geography and cartography, often guides me in the search for unique vantage points and striking visual alignments—for example, photographing Monviso and the Milan skyline from the Bergamo province. Over the years, my projects and images have gained recognition and have been featured in major online outlets and national newspapers, including *La Stampa, Repubblica,* and *Tuttosport*.

Balancing historical reality and imagination with remarkable finesse, Finché tutto splende traces the fascinating lives of the Necchi sisters over eighty years, through moments of joy, sorrow, and unexpected turns. From everyday life to the glamorous social scene of Milan in the 1920s and 1930s, from the dark years of war to the legacy left to the FAI, the novel offers an intimate portrait of a family and the villa that safeguarded their dreams, leaving a lasting mark on the city’s history.
With Lucia Cimini, we will also discuss the 80th anniversary of the Italian Republic.

Gianduja it officially originated at the beginning of the 19th century (around 1804–1808) as a puppet created by the Turin puppeteers Giovanni Battista Sales and Gioachino Bellone. 
The name derives from the Piedmontese expression "Gioann dla doja" → "Giovanni of the tankard" (or "Giovanni of the jug"; doja or douja is the typical Piedmontese wine jug/boccale). It therefore represents a cheerful character, a lover of good wine, good-natured, a bit cunning, seemingly naive but full of common sense, generous, and fond of good company.

Giuseppe Culicchia (Turin, 1965), writer, essayist and translator. Former bookseller, author of numerous successful novels, he is the director of the Fondazione Circolo dei Lettori (April 2025). 
The first edition of Francesissimo — a mirror and complementary project to Italissimo, which for ten years has brought Italian literature and culture to Paris — will take place in Turin from 30 January to 1 February 2026, bringing the French literature and culture festival to the city: meetings with French and francophone authors and author-esses, readings and film screenings, designed to foster dialogue between the cultural world across the Alps and the Italian public.
Francesissimo, conceived by the Fondazione Circolo dei Lettori and the Consulate General of France in Milan, and curated by Fabio Gambaro, will be held at the Circolo dei Lettori e delle Lettrici, Cinema Massimo, Alliance Française Torino, and the Biblioteca Civica Centrale.
The festival opens with Daniel Pennac. It closes with Boualem Sansal: his first public appearance following the pardon he received on 12 November last year from his country, Algeria, where he had been imprisoned since November 2024 for “undermining national unity”.

guests.bio:
Active in the delivery of major international events since 2011, Irene has built extensive experience in Ceremonies, working at senior level as a Cast and Volunteer Manager. In the early years of her career, she held Cast Manager roles across a number of global sporting events, leading the recruitment and management of volunteer performers and talent for Opening and Closing Ceremonies. Her experience includes UEFA EURO 2012, the Baku 2015 European Games, the Jakarta 2015 Asian Para Games, the Baku 2017 Islamic Solidarity Games, and the 5th Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Turkmenistan in 2017.
In 2018, she transitioned from Ceremonies into Volunteer Management, joining the UEFA EURO 2020 Volunteer Programme in Rome. Alongside this role, she continued to collaborate on football-related Ceremonies, including the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations in Gabon, the 2020 African Nations Championship, and the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations in Cameroon. In subsequent years, she also contributed to the delivery of several UEFA competitions, such as the 2019 UEFA European Under-21 Championship, the UEFA Nations League Finals, and the 2022 UEFA Women’s Champions League Final.
She later relocated abroad to work as Deputy Project Director, overseeing operations and delivery for the Islamic Arts Biennale at the Diriyah Biennale Foundation. She is currently involved in the organisation of the Milano Cortina 2026 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games, having contributed from the outset to the planning and development of Team26, the official volunteer programme of Milano Cortina 2026.

guests.bio:
Maurizio Gherardini is the 19th President in the history of Lega Basket Serie A.
He played, served as assistant coach, and was general manager for Libertas Forlì. He then moved to Benetton Treviso (General Manager starting in 1992). During his time in Treviso, the team won four Italian League titles (scudetti), one EuroLeague (Coppa d’Europa), one Saporta Cup, seven Italian Cups, and three Italian Supercups. While at Benetton, Gherardini was voted Best Executive of Lega Basket in 2006 and received the prestigious “Oscar del Basket - Pietro Reverberi” award in 2003. Gherardini was also a member of the FIBA Sports Commission from 1998 to 2000, and served on the EuroLeague board from 2001 to 2006 and from 2014 onward, additionally earning the ‘EuroLeague Executive of the Year’ award in 2017. In 2006, he moved to the NBA, where he served as Vice President and Assistant General Manager of the Toronto Raptors, becoming the first European executive to join an NBA club's front office. During this period, he also spent 7 years as Managing Director of the men's national team sector for the Canadian Basketball Federation and remains a permanent member of Canada Basketball's Council of Excellence. Later, in November 2013, he joined the Oklahoma City Thunder staff as senior advisor and head of international affairs.
From 2014 to 2025, he led the basketball operations at Fenerbahçe Istanbul, winning the EuroLeague in 2017 and 2025, six Turkish Super League titles (scudetti), six Turkish Cups, and three Turkish Presidential Cups (Supercoppe).

(✏️Rosarianna Romano) Una donna «nella scienza». Luisa Torsi, scienziata e docente di Chimica dell'Università di Bari, è stata inserita da Unesco tra le donne che hanno contribuito in modo significativo all’avanzamento della conoscenza delle materie scientifiche. “Women in science: a journey through the discoveries and challenges of women scientists across history and the world” è infatti la mostra dedicata alle scienziate che hanno sostenuto l’avanzamento del sapere in diversi ambiti disciplinari. «Sono incredibilmente orgogliosa di essere menzionata dall'Unesco nella loro mostra “Women in Science: a journey through the discoveries and challenges of women scientists across history and the world”, insieme a donne pionieristiche che hanno plasmato la scienza e dato contributi innovativi in vari campi», ha scritto Torsi sul suo profilo Facebook. L’iniziativa si colloca all’interno del museo virtuale della scienza Unesco, piattaforma globale nata nell’ambito del decennio internazionale delle scienze per lo sviluppo sostenibile, con l’obiettivo di promuovere un accesso aperto, inclusivo e globale alla cultura scientifica. E, nello stesso tempo, di supportare l’educazione Stem (Science, technology, engineering and mathematics) attraverso vari strumenti e risorse.

guests.bio: Massimiliano Lisa is the Director and co-founder of the Museo Leonardo3 in Milan, an interactive museum devoted to the genius of Leonardo da Vinci. Opened in 2013 in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, the museum is known for reconstructing working machines directly from Leonardo’s original drawings. Under Lisa’s direction, researchers and engineers have recreated many of these designs, helping visitors understand how Leonardo imagined technology centuries ahead of its time. With a background in journalism, publishing and digital media, Lisa has spent many years combining technology and cultural heritage. Through the Leonardo3 research centre, he works on interpreting Leonardo’s manuscripts and transforming them into physical models and digital experiences. Among the museum’s most fascinating projects are the reconstructions of Leonardo’s mechanical clocks and timekeeping devices.

guests.bio: Daniela Tommasini is an Italian researcher and writer with a long-standing connection to Greenland and Arctic communities. Since her first journey to Greenland in the 1990s, she has regularly returned to the island, building close relationships with local communities. Her work combines academic research with personal storytelling about everyday life in the Arctic. Through her writings and public talks, she offers a unique perspective on cultures, landscapes, and the challenges of living in one of the most remote places on Earth. guests.bio:
A very large community surrounds Ugolize, which in recent years has managed to win the affection of a wide audience—from Generation Z to the under-35s and even older generations. This is largely thanks to the ironic tone of their content, which is always able to spark awareness while simultaneously encouraging reflection on important social issues in our increasingly globalized societies.

Ugolize have also released their book *“Ugolize: Avventure fuori dagli schemi”* (*Ugolize: Adventures Off the Beaten Path*), a perfect read for getting a laugh even after a terrible day. It features an endless stream of witty one-liners, with the spotlight on original and entertaining cartoons starring the round-headed little characters that have made so many people laugh on social media.

The themes explored by Ugolize range from everyday life to contemporary challenges, with particular attention to common situations that intertwine irony and social reality. Among the main topics they address are generational differences, the paradoxes of the workplace, and current social issues such as climate change and technology—along with reflective and humorous insights that are always presented through a carefully tailored generational lens.

guests.bio:
By David Lawrence and Francesco Longo
Photographs that tell the story of the artist through the eyes of his brother Terry Burns.
Ninety photographs construct a narrative about David Bowie that begins with a private relationship and spans the artist’s entire public trajectory. David Bowie, My Brother is a project by writer David Lawrence, presented for the first time in Italy—after its exhibition in Paris—from April 17 to July 12 at Musa Art Gallery in Turin. 
The perspective is defined by the exhibition’s structure: the figure of Terry Burns, Bowie’s half-brother, becomes the lens through which images, texts, and materials are interpreted. Not a retrospective, but a journey that connects biographical episodes, cultural references, and the construction of artistic identity

guests.bio:
Sean Albain was born in Glasgow in 1988. After a troubled youth, he left Scotland at fifteen and fell into heroin use in Ireland. His father’s death became a turning point: he returned to Glasgow, worked in bars, and studied theatre. At twenty, he set off for Africa with a guitar, traveling and performing across Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and South Africa. After a failed attempt to reach India, he moved to Southeast Asia in 2011, living on the streets through hardship and danger.
He later returned to Europe and settled in Milan, where he performed at the Colonne di San Lorenzo and began his music career. During the Covid period, he taught English online and studied psychology and philosophy. He now lives in Dovera (Lombardy), where he teaches and writes. His debut album, You’ll Be Fine, reflects his nomadic and challenging life journey.

Benjamin Pritchard is a British para-rower. He won the gold medal in the men’s PR1 single sculls at the 2024 Summer Paralympics and also claimed gold at the 2025 European Rowing Championships, setting a world record.

A former cyclist and triathlete, Benjamin’s journey took an unexpected turn when he became paralysed from the waist down following a cycling crash in September 2016. During his rehabilitation at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, he discovered indoor rowing, quickly catching the attention of British Rowing staff. He joined the para development squad in 2017 and has never looked back.

His natural talent and dedication propelled him onto the international stage, making his GB Rowing Team debut in the PR1 men’s single sculls at the 2019 World Championships. After finishing fifth at the delayed Tokyo Paralympic Games—where he set a Paralympic record—he continued his rise, securing two World Championship podium finishes. In 2024, he became Paralympic Champion in Paris, setting another Paralympic record in the process.

Beyond his achievements on the water, Benjamin is a passionate advocate for athletes, representing their voices on both the World Rowing and British Paralympic Association Athletes’ Commissions. He is also gaining experience in two of his passions—coffee and BBC local radio. He is married to Meg and is a proud father to Efa.

A very large community surrounds Ugolize, which in recent years has managed to win the affection of a wide audience—from Generation Z to the under-35s and even older generations. This is largely thanks to the ironic tone of their content, which is always able to spark awareness while simultaneously encouraging reflection on important social issues in our increasingly globalized societies.

Ugolize have also released their book *“Ugolize: Avventure fuori dagli schemi”* (*Ugolize: Adventures Off the Beaten Path*), a perfect read for getting a laugh even after a terrible day. It features an endless stream of witty one-liners, with the spotlight on original and entertaining cartoons starring the round-headed little characters that have made so many people laugh on social media.

The themes explored by Ugolize range from everyday life to contemporary challenges, with particular attention to common situations that intertwine irony and social reality. Among the main topics they address are generational differences, the paradoxes of the workplace, and current social issues such as climate change and technology—along with reflective and humorous insights that are always presented through a carefully tailored generational lens.

Through her writings and public talks, she offers a unique perspective on cultures, landscapes, and the challenges of living in one of the most remote places on Earth. guests.bio:
Maurizio Gherardini is the 19th President in the history of Lega Basket Serie A.
He played, served as assistant coach, and was general manager for Libertas Forlì. He then moved to Benetton Treviso (General Manager starting in 1992). During his time in Treviso, the team won four Italian League titles (scudetti), one EuroLeague (Coppa d’Europa), one Saporta Cup, seven Italian Cups, and three Italian Supercups. While at Benetton, Gherardini was voted Best Executive of Lega Basket in 2006 and received the prestigious “Oscar del Basket - Pietro Reverberi” award in 2003. Gherardini was also a member of the FIBA Sports Commission from 1998 to 2000, and served on the EuroLeague board from 2001 to 2006 and from 2014 onward, additionally earning the ‘EuroLeague Executive of the Year’ award in 2017. In 2006, he moved to the NBA, where he served as Vice President and Assistant General Manager of the Toronto Raptors, becoming the first European executive to join an NBA club's front office. During this period, he also spent 7 years as Managing Director of the men's national team sector for the Canadian Basketball Federation and remains a permanent member of Canada Basketball's Council of Excellence. Later, in November 2013, he joined the Oklahoma City Thunder staff as senior advisor and head of international affairs.
From 2014 to 2025, he led the basketball operations at Fenerbahçe Istanbul, winning the EuroLeague in 2017 and 2025, six Turkish Super League titles (scudetti), six Turkish Cups, and three Turkish Presidential Cups (Supercoppe).

Giuseppe Culicchia (Turin, 1965), writer, essayist and translator. Former bookseller, author of numerous successful novels, he is the director of the Fondazione Circolo dei Lettori (April 2025). 
The first edition of Francesissimo — a mirror and complementary project to Italissimo, which for ten years has brought Italian literature and culture to Paris — will take place in Turin from 30 January to 1 February 2026, bringing the French literature and culture festival to the city: meetings with French and francophone authors and author-esses, readings and film screenings, designed to foster dialogue between the cultural world across the Alps and the Italian public.
Francesissimo, conceived by the Fondazione Circolo dei Lettori and the Consulate General of France in Milan, and curated by Fabio Gambaro, will be held at the Circolo dei Lettori e delle Lettrici, Cinema Massimo, Alliance Française Torino, and the Biblioteca Civica Centrale.
The festival opens with Daniel Pennac. It closes with Boualem Sansal: his first public appearance following the pardon he received on 12 November last year from his country, Algeria, where he had been imprisoned since November 2024 for “undermining national unity”.

My academic background, along with a strong passion for geography and cartography, often guides me in the search for unique vantage points and striking visual alignments—for example, photographing Monviso and the Milan skyline from the Bergamo province. Artissima is Italy’s most important contemporary art fair. Since its establishment in 1994, it has combined the presence of an international market with a focus on experimentation and research.
Galleries from around the world participate every year. In addition to the 4 flaghisp sections (Main Section, Monologue/Dialogue, New Entries, Art Spaces & Editions), Artissima is also composed of 3 curated sections, headed by a board of international curators and museum directors, devoted to emerging artists (Present Future), to the rediscovery of the pioneers of contemporary art (Back to the Future) and to the drawing (Disegni). In 2025, the fair will be hosted from 31 October to 2 November (30 October preview by invitation) in Torino.

Luca  Corlatti, Scientific coordinator for Stelvio Park in Lombardy Region, where he lworks for Office of Scientific Research and Our activities focusing on biodiversity and climate change monitoring, relationships between biodiversity abd human-environment and applied applied research on keystone Alpine species, which includes Cervus Elaphus, the Red Deer, Cervo Nobile in italian. Deer had (almost) completely disappeared from Italy after World War II.
 Now the species is in a good state of conservation. The deer is the largest wild ruminant herbivore in Italy. In many areas, especially in parks and protected areas, numbers and densities are very high. This has a significant impact on vegetation, so much so that the deer is referred to as the engineer of ecosystems. Now, with the spontaneous return of the wolf to the Alps, we are entering a new phase of ecosystem balance. The arrival of the predator may change the numbers and behavior of prey, and this, in turn, may have an effect on vegetation. The study of trophic cascades in parks and its usefulness.

Luca Bruschi is the director of AEVF, European Association of the Via Francigena Ways. As Director, Bruschi is at the forefront of the nomination of the Via Francigena as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July, the preliminary dossier was officially submitted in Paris, focusing on the Italian section of the route from the Great St. Bernard Pass to Rome. The next stage of the candidacy will begin at the end of September 2025: this phase involves compiling the final dossier, identifying the cultural assets to be included on the UNESCO list, producing detailed cartography, and organizing participatory meetings with local communities along the route.The Via Francigena is certified Cultural Route of the Council of Europe. More than 3000 kilometers, from Canterbury to Rome and Santa Maria di Leuca, to walk step by step on mountain paths, mule tracks, rural and secondary roads, cypress-lined dirt roads or among majestic pines. Bruschi has personally completed the Via Francigena, the Camino de Santiago, and many other pilgrimage routes and cultural itineraries across Europe.

Fabio Testi is the star who turned his good looks from a supposed “flaw” into a ticket to cinematic legend. Born in Peschiera del Garda, he started out as a stuntman — falling off horses, crashing motorbikes, and even hanging in midair for two weeks on the set of Barbarella. It was Vittorio De Sica who catapulted him to fame with the Oscar-winning The Garden of the Finzi-Continis in 1970. From there came a career packed with auteur films and popular hits (Addio fratello crudele, L’important c’est d’aimer with Romy Schneider, Camorra by Pasquale Squitieri), over a hundred screen and stage credits, and a love life straight out of the tabloids — Ursula Andress, Anita Ekberg, Charlotte Rampling, Edwige Fenech… Today, well into his eighties, Testi still keeps us guessing: he grows truffles by Lake Garda, tours with a poetry-and-music show, and pops up in international cinema — most recently in Reflet dans un diamant mort, which premiered at the Berlinale. Always elegant, always magnetic, he’s living proof that yes, there really are a few beautiful men who are also smart.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Professor SERGIO STEFANNI: Born in Desenzano del Garda (Italy) on 29/12/1967, after a Master Degree in marine studies at University of Genoa and a PhD at the School of Biological Science at the University of Bristol, he has been a researcher at Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn in Naples (Italy) since 2016. His research interests are molecular ecology, population genetics and phylogeny of marine organisms. He study mainly fish and sharks, from coastal to the deep-sea, but he's been a guest of Paparazzi helping our understanding of marine alien species in our seas like the lionfish and the silver-cheeked toadfish. ANDREA LEVY: Andrea Levy was born in Ancona on July 7, 1971. He specialized in international marketing and communication at the University of Nevada. His passion for cars has been with him since childhood. He grew up in Moncalieri, near Turin, where he saw prototypes and cars from legendary coachbuilders and manufacturers—Pininfarina, Giugiaro, Italdesign, and Fiat—come to life and hit the roads. Today, he is a successful entrepreneur in communication and events, a devoted collector of sports cars and supercars, and a true motorsport enthusiast. He races with Ferrari Club Italia and competes in Time Attack with Ferrari, Radical, and Dallara. Always on the move, he follows racing competitions, auto shows, and dynamic events such as Goodwood and Pebble Beach—experiences that sparked the idea behind the Salone dell'Auto format, which has now also evolved into the Milano Monza Motor Show.
